strengths: The paper explores a useful application of learned edit-distance embeddings to short quaternary code design. Algorithm 1 uses exact radius-two exclusion, so the constructed codebook's minimum-distance guarantee does not depend on embedding accuracy.

Table 1 shows consistent improvements over random selection across ten runs, with variability and a loss-function ablation reported. At n=11, the best codebook contains 36,368 words versus 31,142 for random selection, a 16.8% cardinality improvement.

The decoder receives substantial empirical testing: querying four candidates produces zero reported failures in 10^8 random single-edit trials at each tested length. The measured speedups over the implemented brute-force baseline are encouraging.

The algorithm and overall workflow are reasonably clear. Synthetic data generation, a source-code link, and acknowledgment of construction scalability limitations are helpful. No material research ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: The central density argument in Section 4.2 is unjustified. Batch normalization does not make embeddings multivariate Gaussian, and low fitted Gaussian density is not shown to predict the number of conflicting sequences remaining during search. The binary t-SNE visualization cannot establish these relationships. Greedy selection also does not guarantee maximum codebook size.

The headline claim of reliable O(n) decoding is unsupported. The k=1 setting has approximately 0.33–0.83% failures, while the more reliable multiple-candidate setting includes verification that Section 5.5 itself assigns O(n^2) complexity. Moreover, logarithmic expected k-d-tree query time requires assumptions not established for these 64-dimensional embeddings. Randomized success is strong empirical evidence, but does not certify correction of every single-edit input.

The decoding baseline is unnecessarily restrictive. For a single-edit channel, one can enumerate O(n) possible corrected strings and query a hashed codebook, avoiding a scan through every codeword. Thresholded edit-distance algorithms also avoid the relevance of the general quadratic-hardness argument. Without suitable exact bounded-distance baselines, the claimed computational advantage remains unclear.

The optimality and state-of-the-art claims exceed the evidence. Matching a proposed redundancy curve over a few short lengths does not establish proximity to the finite-length optimum; the substitution-only lower bound does not establish the additional log-log term. Comparisons need stronger short-length codebook searches, such as degree-based greedy selection or local search. The learning-specific improvement at n=11 is about 1.02 percentage points in code rate over random selection.

The segmented-channel motivation is not validated end to end. Experiments supply isolated segments containing exactly one edit, without demonstrating boundary recovery in a concatenated stream, synchronization overhead, or performance with multiple errors and an outer code. Consequently, improvements in overall storage rate and practical multiple-error correction remain unestablished.

Reproducibility and efficiency reporting are incomplete in the manuscript. Important omissions include training-pair sampling, optimization settings, variable-length input handling, hardware, and whether timings include embedding and exact verification. Training, exhaustive codebook construction, initialization time, and peak memory are also unreported, preventing assessment of the full computational tradeoff even at the tested lengths.
